en: If you grew into a mighty hero,
The equal of any hero's son,
I believed you would bring turmoil
Upon Beijing.
From the mouth of the treasury,
I truly fashioned this battle-axe
From ore of Kaiypchy-Too.
Upon the Argyn and Kyrgyz
I laid much hardship;
From the Argyn and Kyrgyz
I exacted tribute by force.
Unable to withstand the charcoal it consumed,
Many forests were destroyed;
Unable to withstand its bellows,
Many young bulls were slaughtered.
I had its point forged sharp,
And heated its joined edge red.
So that wherever it struck would not remain whole,
But would flare and burn away,
In a dragon's venom
I tempered it sixty times.
Once swung, it did not draw back;
It was not stopped by steel.
When swung, it seemed to lengthen;
In the struggle the battle-axe
Glowed red as an ember.
I wound its cheek with gold
And destined it for the campaign
Against the seething infidel,
Hero Khan Kongurbai.
If you strike with it, no regret will remain;
If you go and bring great strife
Upon the seething infidel,
Hero Khan Kongurbai.
I had its wrist-loop nailed fast,
Calling the axe a surpassing companion,
So that he would take it especially,
Charge upon the swarming Chinese,
And unleash strife.
So that my only one, whose heart holds vengeance,
Might avenge himself upon the Kalcha,
Made especially for close combat,
I have this axe I fashioned;
And, my only one, hear this too!
When the reins draw side by side,
He may draw it from its sheath;
When the struggle grows fierce,
He may plunge it into the short ribs—
For this purpose I have made it.
Its pommel is gold and its handle brass;
Its length is half a fathom.
Its sheath bears an engraved inscription;
Made fit for war,
It bears the name Aktinte.
So that he may enter the encircling fight
Against infidels numerous as ants,
I fitted it perfectly for my only one;
So that on a desperate day
He might thrust it into the belly,
And, finding the enemy's opening,
Split him apart in terror.
Fashioned to suit you,
I have this fitting gift for you;
Recognize this service
Of your sworn father, the master smith!
And if I speak further, here is another tale:
While your father Manas lived,
Six sharp blades that fell from heaven—
Six accursed things raised among commoners—
Were handled shamefully,
Their cases split, trampled by horses,
Cast upon the ground to rust.
While bloodthirsty Manas lived,
Those six blades sated with blood—
I repaired what rust had eaten,
And fitted them even better
Than when sovereign Manas lived.
For the keen iron and steel,
On account of those six blades,
I endured and lost much.
If he swings one even at stone,
May my only one left by the bloodletter
Split it in two without stopping;
May he see the worth
Of his sworn father, the master smith.
Smashing the Chinese to pieces,
Its edge shortened when swung,
But when he swung it with a cry,
It lengthened to forty gez;
The six sharp blades never sated with blood—
When you battle Beijing,
My hero, my only one, I have these for you!
Against the Chinese you confront,
Let him hang one at his wrist;
Shouting the battle cry “Khan Manas!”
Let him strike the foe without tiring.
Let him reach the one he faces,
Drenching it in bright-red blood,
And pass on after wreaking slaughter;
Let the enemy who challenges him panic.
If Kongurbai should see him,
Let him lose his wits;
Saying, “The bloodletter’s true son!”
Let him flee inside Kakan.
I have prepared these gifts with care;
Take the sword with its sheath,
And enter among the Chinese without looking back,
Bringing alarm wherever you reach!
I fashioned Syrnaiza with full skill,
And, my only one, I have this too!
On the spur of the broken mountain,
At the point of the swelling mountain,
If they stand facing one another,
If they level their spears firmly,
And fight where they meet,
Let him thrust it straight and unwavering;
Let it bring mighty alarm.
If he comes face to face with the Kalcha,
Let him spear through his backbone;
Upon that notorious Kalcha swine,
Let him avenge the valiant hero,
And upon Beijing, lying vast and still,
Let him bring alarm in full measure.
This is the spear I fashioned;
My lord, my only prince, listen well!
The birch of stony ground—
I searched and had the finest cut;
To let it season in its bark,
I had it stacked in the shade.
I passed it from craftsman to craftsman,
Had careful judges test it,
And, to straighten every crooked place,
Had it pressed in a jig.
I had a woodworker shape it,
Plane away every knotted place,
And forty Kalchas finish it.
I surpassed my former craftsmanship;
Fearing it might suddenly break,
I had brass bound around it in four places.
Around the places left exposed,
The forty Kalchas, heeding my words,
Wrapped it with sinew;
When glue was poured within it,
Much of Bölökbai’s treasure
Was consumed.
Fearing it might suddenly break,
I had it covered with elephant hide;
Fearing blood might make it rot,
Below the spear’s tuft
I had it faced with leather.
So it would not slip from the hand,
And would not bring disaster,
I had the handgrip roughened,
And had the handgrip painted.
Its tuft was tipped like a sword;
The value of this single spear
Was fixed at eighty argymaks.
Kongurbai’s blue coat of mail,
That strong armor no bullet pierces—
Let one thrust pierce it;
When driven with the fist, let it sink softly
All the way to its base.
I made its wolf-tongue point barbed,
And set the tip jutting out.
To make it surpassingly keen,
I tempered it with Albaras steel.
So the child might know my worth,
If he drives it against black stone,
Let it enter like mud.
If the two sides take their stands,
Firing guns and drawing bows,
And fight without fleeing,
Let the splendid hero, the bloodletter’s son,
Enter battle without tiring;
Let him truly level the spear,
And, if the Black Chinese stand firm,
Pursue them screaming.
When he faces a determined foe,
At the sight of the gray wolf’s son,
Let them fail to endure and be ruined.
I made Syrnaiza as a gift;
When you bring turmoil to Beijing,
When you go to the Kakanchin,
Accept it as a gift.
When you strike the foe you face,
My only one, the valiant man’s son,
Drink your fill of joy;
Thinking of your poor sworn father,
Keep us within your heart!
The Kakanchin is the foe you will fight;
Splendid hero, son of the bloodletter,
Go and unleash havoc!
Let me give you the weapons of war;
Splendid hero, son of the bloodletter,
Take them without haste or confusion!
There is no end to my treasury;
In the gathered treasury
Of your sworn father, the master smith,
What is there, and what is not!
I knew the Black Chinese Kakanchin
Would be the foe you fought;
I long believed that the orphaned hero,
The bloodletter’s son,
Would avenge himself upon the teeming Black Chinese.
I give Syrnaiza as a gift;
My hero, take it gladly.
Meet them and fight,
And bring turmoil to Beijing!
Strike that swine, Lord Kongurbai,
And crush him like chaff;
Cut off his head, bind it on,
And bring it specially as a gift
To your sworn father, the master smith!
My orphan, son of the keen warrior,
Gird your waist with perfect skill!
Against the Chinese who cover the earth,
Enter alone and attack.
Beijing, where no frail old man can tread—
Disgrace if you let yourself be defeated there.
You wild youth who takes refuge,
Your life is entrusted to God!
Against the Chinese who throng the earth,
You have set out alone on holy war;
Upon the toilsome Black Chinese,
You intend to pursue the blood-price.
May your news come from the campaign,
May your journey lead back from Beijing;
A hero’s work is risk itself—
You are going forth to meet it!
The Kakanchin is the foe you will fight;
God knows whether you will die,
God knows whether you will return—
You are going forth to die!
You have begun the journey to Beijing,
Leaving the many Argyn and Kyrgyz people,
Leaving your camp desolate!
They say Beijing is a distant land,
One no one has seen from afar;
For a traveler who goes without tiring,
They say the road is six months long.
If one circles Great Beijing,
It has a lake that takes long to traverse;
If one goes straight, some roads
Cross a desert forty days wide.
Beijing is no cheap and easy land,
No people of Andizhan
To be taken and left gaping.
My beloved one who gives me comfort,
Go safely and return unharmed;
Come back quickly and do not make us pine!
Hero Bölökbai said these words,
Then all the equipment from the treasury
He gave and entrusted to him;
The infidel spoke in lament,
And every weapon of war
He entrusted to Semetey.
